Name: Gadir at the Pillars of Hercules: Ancient Phoenician City and the Silver Sea Route
RagShortTexts: Gadir is the oldest Phoenician colony in the western Mediterranean and directly controls the strait leading to the Atlantic
The ever-burning sacred fire of the temple of Melqart witnessed Hannibal's oath before his campaign and the rites of the Barca family
It is an unsinkable floating trading island that ships Andalusian minerals and Atlantic tin
BaseText: Gadir (town_carthage_gadir, modern Cadiz) was founded by Phoenicians from Tyre in the eleventh century BC and is the oldest continuously inhabited city in Western Europe. It lies on a long, narrow chain of sandy islands off the mouth of the Guadalquivir, facing the surging currents of the Atlantic across the water, and guards the vital western gate of the Pillars of Hercules (the Strait of Gibraltar). The city's temple of Melqart was famous for its twin bronze pillars and a sacred fire that had not gone out for a thousand years, and it was here that Hannibal swore to overthrow Rome before setting out on his march north. Gadir was not only the export port for the rich silver and olive oil of Andalusia, but also a strategic hub linking the sea route to the tin mines of Britain. Near the end of the war Mago, commander at Gadir, abandoned the city and withdrew, and the city at once concluded a treaty of peace and alliance with Rome.

Variants.Content: The incense smoke of the temple of Melqart protects the bloodline of seafarers. Setting sail from Gadir, the purple sails of Phoenicia can reach the ocean at the end of the world and the tin islands.
Uprooting Gadir cuts Carthage's last foothold in Iberia for good. The silver of Spain will now be escorted to the treasury by Roman quinqueremes instead.

We are merchants, not guardians of any creed. Whether the purple banner or the eagle standard flies over the walls, as long as the Atlantic tides keep flowing, the altar of Melqart will always be offered silver coins.
